extracted.intended_audience: 17th-century natural philosophers, mathematicians, and scholarly librarians (readers of the Philosophical Transactions / Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for assembling, selecting, and preserving mathematical and related scientific works and instruments (what to collect, how many, how to present them, and what to preserve). Targeted to scholars, librarians, and those compiling scientific collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select only the best and most deserving works
rubrics_metrics.description: “it seems to me more advisable to select only the best and most deserving of them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer high-quality, authoritative authors and works (e.g., Euclid, Apollonius, Archimedes, Theodosius, Pappus, Ptolemy; moderns like Viète, Clavius, Herigonius). Use judgement to prefer fundamental, exemplary texts rather than attempting to collect everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose concise, clear treatises for each science
rubrics_metrics.description: “each of them might compose a treatise on a science, in one clear and convenient volume; such things being supplied as are wanting in others, and unnecessary things being omitted; we might doubtless have in 12 volumes, in a short and nervous manner, all that could be desired in this matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volumes should be concise, focused, fill known gaps, and omit superfluous verbosity. Aim for clarity and compactness so a single volume can serve as a usable summary of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include representative canonical authors per subfield (set counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for numbers and selections: e.g., ‘for mathematics... might be comprehended in those 12 volumes’; for ‘fortification and music, eight or ten authors’; for mechanical subjects, forces of motion, machines, and water-works, about 10 or 12 authors’ etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the collection with explicit targets per subject (suggested counts and exemplar names are provided). Use these counts as a practical bound to create a comprehensive yet manageable library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve at least one copy of even trivial or erroneous works
rubrics_metrics.description: “the most trivial writing, or mathematical instrument, ought to be preserved, one copy at least, even for its errors”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep copies of lesser works and imperfect instruments because they can contain useful hints, pedagogical redundancy (tautologies useful to some learners), evidence of historical practice, and instructive errors. Such preservation aids future invention and scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer judgment over exhaustive diligence in collecting
rubrics_metrics.description: “diligence in collecting all things is not so necessary, as judgment to reject what is superfluous, and knowledge to supply such things as are not yet discovered.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not aim to amass every existing text; instead apply critical judgement to exclude the superfluous and identify what genuinely needs to be added. Curatorial discernment is more valuable than mere accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit physical apparatus to a few best, most useful instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: “As to mathematical instruments, it would be of little consequence to have an apparatus consisting of all that have hitherto been invented. It might be sufficient to have four or five of the best of their kind, and those of the most convenient and useful sorts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than stockpiling every instrument, acquire a small set of high-quality, versatile instruments that exemplify the state of the art and are practical for use and demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and describe instruments rather than owning all
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is sufficient if he can describe them all, and that he either knows how to make for himself such as are wanted, or can direct artificers to construct them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ownership is impractical, ensure accurate descriptions, plans, or instructions are available so instruments can be reproduced or constructed when needed. Emphasize know-how and descriptions over physical possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage originality and deter plagiarism through comprehensive records
rubrics_metrics.description: “men of candour and ingenuity... when they see so many have gone before them, on almost every subject, will be cautious not to produce any thing to the public, but what is new and their own invention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive, accessible collection helps authors see prior work and thereby promotes originality, discourages plagiarism, and raises the overall standard of publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize varied learner needs; include repetitious or elementary treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: “there are some persons who can understand nothing, unless repeated to them a hundred times... those tautologies are well adapted to such persons... the same things being not equally known to all; we must therefore make very different beginnings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate materials at multiple levels: include elementary, repetitive, and remedial texts as well as advanced treatises to serve diverse learners and educational roles (monitors/teachers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the 'self-sufficient' mathematician: balance history and investigative skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes' distinction: ‘By the history I mean whatever is already discovered, and is committed to books. And by the science, the skill of resolving all questions... He who possesses this faculty, has but little need of other assistance, and may therefore be properly called self-sufficient.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value both comprehensive knowledge of extant results (the historical record) and the practical skill to solve new problems. Education and the library should aim to develop investigators who can both consult the record and independently advance the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a universal library as a cure for frivolous scribbling and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: “the complete collection... seems to me to be quite necessary... the less I am pleased with these minute mathematicians, the more I should wish for a library of this kind, as being the only method of curing that licentious itch of scribbling... the plagiaries... will not have the impudence to vend, as their own, any old books.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a well-curated, comprehensive bibliographic repository will elevate standards by exposing weak or plagiarized work, discouraging trivial publication, and guiding prospective authors toward substantive contributions.
